prompt: The ring has six networks. Using static routes only, how many routes would the four routers need in total so that every router reaches every network?
hint: Each router needs one route per network it is not connected to.

prompt: What does a link-state router send that a distance-vector router does not?
hint: One sends opinions, the other sends facts.

choices.text: Its whole routing table, sent to each neighbour every 30 seconds
choices.why: That is what RIP, a distance-vector protocol, sends.

choices.text: Hello packets to find neighbours
choices.why: Both families use hellos; RIP is the exception that relies on its updates alone.

choices.text: Its distance to each destination
choices.why: Distances are what distance vector shares. Link state shares links and lets each router work out distances.

choices.text: A description of its own links, to every router in the area
choices.why: Right. Every router gets the same descriptions and builds the same map.

prompt: Match each protocol to its administrative distance, as lesson 14 listed them.
hint: Lower is more believed.

prompt: Why are RIP, OSPF and EIGRP not used between two different companies on the internet?
hint: What do interior protocols assume about every router?

choices.text: They do not carry IPv4 public addresses
choices.why: They carry any prefix. Addresses are not the obstacle.

choices.text: They trust every router to tell the truth
choices.why: Right. Between organisations that trust is missing, which is why BGP exists.

choices.text: They exceed fifteen hops between companies
choices.why: Fifteen is RIP's limit alone, and not the reason for the boundary.

choices.text: They need a cable between every pair of routers
choices.why: This lesson's ring has no such cables, and every protocol in it worked.

prompt: In `show ip rip` on r1, 10.20.2.0/24 appears with metric 2 from 10.20.0.2. Why 2?
hint: What did r2 say, and what did r1 add?

choices.text: r2 reported 1 for its own network and r1 added 1
choices.why: Right. A connected network counts 1, and each router adds one.

choices.text: Two cables lie between r1 and pc2's network
choices.why: RIP counts routers, not cables, though here the numbers happen to coincide for a different reason.

choices.text: The route was learned twice, once from each neighbour
choices.why: The metric is a distance, not a count of offers.

choices.text: It is the kernel's metric divided by ten
choices.why: The kernel's 20 is a number FRR writes on every route, unrelated to RIP.

prompt: In RIP, what metric means that a network is unreachable?
hint: One more than the largest usable distance.

prompt: r1's `show ip rip` shows `02:55` in the Time column for a route learned from r2. What happens if r2 stops sending updates and the countdown reaches zero?
hint: Updates every 30 seconds refresh it.

choices.text: r1 asks r2 to resend the route
choices.why: RIP does not ask. It waits for the next update and gives up when none comes.

choices.text: Nothing, because a route from a neighbour is kept until the neighbour withdraws it
choices.why: A dead neighbour withdraws nothing. The timer is how RIP notices it is dead.

choices.text: The metric is raised by one for each minute of silence
choices.why: Silence does not add hops. The route is either refreshed or invalid.

choices.text: The route is declared invalid, 180 seconds after it was last heard
choices.why: Right. The timer is RIP's only way of noticing a neighbour that went quiet.

prompt: Imagine the cable from r1 to r2 is a slow 2 Mbit/s line and the three other cables are 10 Gbit/s. Which path does RIP choose from pc1 to pc2, and why?
hint: What is RIP's metric made of?

choices.text: Round the ring, because it measures the speed of each link
choices.why: RIP measures nothing about links. That is what OSPF's cost and EIGRP's bandwidth are for.

choices.text: The slow direct line, because it is fewer routers away
choices.why: Right. One hop beats three, whatever the hops are made of.

choices.text: Both, splitting the traffic by speed
choices.why: RIP would split only between paths of equal hop count, and these are not equal.

choices.text: Neither, because the slow line makes the ring inconsistent
choices.why: Speed differences are normal and RIP does not see them at all.

prompt: r1 lists both OSPF neighbours as `Full/-`. What does `Full` mean?
hint: It is the last state of the list.

choices.text: The link to that neighbour is at full capacity
choices.why: OSPF states describe the conversation between routers, not the traffic on the cable.

choices.text: The two routers hold identical databases
choices.why: Right. Full is reached after the exchange and loading states.

choices.text: That neighbour has been elected designated router
choices.why: The role is the part after the slash, and it is empty: the links are point-to-point.

choices.text: The neighbour has reached the maximum number of routes
choices.why: OSPF has no such limit in its neighbour states.

prompt: Put these OSPF neighbour states in the order a new neighbour passes through them.
hint: Hear it, agree, swap summaries, fetch the rest, done.
trap: ExStart comes before Exchange: the two routers first agree who leads the exchange, then exchange.

prompt: r3 has two point-to-point OSPF cables and no LAN. How many links does its router LSA list?
hint: Each point-to-point cable is described as two things.

prompt: A new router is added to the ring with a hello interval of 1 second and a dead interval of 4, while its neighbour keeps 10 and 40. What do you see on the neighbour?
hint: What has to match before two routers become neighbours?

choices.text: An adjacency that comes up and agrees on the faster timers
choices.why: OSPF does not negotiate timers. A mismatch stops the adjacency forming.

choices.text: An error message naming the mismatched timers on r1's console
choices.why: The section's point is that the symptom is an absence, not a message.

choices.text: The two never form an adjacency
choices.why: Right. Mismatched hello or dead intervals mean the routers never become neighbours.

choices.text: A neighbour that flaps between Full and Down every 4 seconds
choices.why: It never reaches Full in the first place.

prompt: From r1 to 10.20.2.0/24 over the direct cable, with cost 100 on that cable and 10 on r2's interface on pc2's network, what is the total OSPF cost?
hint: Add the interfaces the packet leaves by.

prompt: Suppose the cost on the r1–r2 cable were lowered from 100 to 25, with every other interface still at 10. What would r1's OSPF cost to 10.20.2.0/24 become?
hint: Compute both paths and keep the lower.
One is the same on every OSPF line.

choices.text: Hop count and time in seconds
choices.why: OSPF counts neither hops nor seconds in that bracket.

choices.text: The cost through r4 and the cost through r2
choices.why: The direct path costs 110 by coincidence of numbers, but the bracket holds one route's values.

choices.text: Administrative distance and path cost
choices.why: Right. 110 is OSPF's distance, the same on every line; 40 is the cost of this path.

choices.text: The area number and the router's priority
choices.why: The area is 0 and priorities are in the neighbour table.

prompt: Starting from this lab, the cost on the r3–r4 cable is raised from 10 to 80 at both ends. What does r1 do with traffic for 10.20.2.0/24?
hint: Add up both paths again. What if they are equal?

choices.text: It keeps the path through r4, which was chosen first
choices.why: OSPF recalculates on every change; having been first gives a path nothing.

choices.text: It moves everything to the direct cable
choices.why: The direct path is 110, and the long way is now 10 + 80 + 10 + 10 = 110 too, so neither is lower.

choices.text: It drops the traffic until an engineer picks a path
choices.why: Equal paths are not a conflict for OSPF.

choices.text: Both paths now cost 110, so it uses both
choices.why: Right. Equal totals mean OSPF installs both and splits the traffic.

prompt: In `show ip route ospf`, the line `O   10.20.0.0/30 [110/100] is directly connected, eth1` has no `>` and no `*`. Why is it not used?
hint: What else does r1 know about its own cable?

choices.text: The connected route for that cable has distance 0 and wins
choices.why: Right. OSPF knows it, but the connected source is believed first.

choices.text: Its cost of 100 is too high to be installed
choices.why: There is no ceiling on cost; this is about competing sources.

choices.text: The neighbour on eth1 is down
choices.why: r2 was Full on eth1 when this was printed.

choices.text: OSPF installs a route only after it has been stable for a minute
choices.why: Other OSPF lines with the same age carry `>*`.

prompt: pc1's ping sent 70 packets, one per second, and got 40 replies. About how many seconds was there no path between pc1 and pc2?
hint: Each lost packet is one second.

prompt: Twenty seconds after the cut, r1 still listed r4 as Full with 8.651s of dead time left. Why had r1 not noticed the failure?
hint: What tells OSPF a neighbour is gone, when the interface stays up?

choices.text: r4 kept sending hellos through the failed device
choices.why: Nothing crossed the failed link in either direction.

choices.text: OSPF checks neighbours once a minute
choices.why: There is no periodic check; there is a dead timer reset by each hello.

choices.text: The interface still had its signal, so only the 40-second dead timer could reveal it
choices.why: Right. With the signal up, OSPF waits out the dead interval.

choices.text: The retransmission list was full
choices.why: RXmtL 2 shows two pending updates; it is a symptom, not a cause.

prompt: An engineer wants the ring to recover from a silent failure in under a second. Which change does the lesson point to?
hint: Lesson 3's timers are faster than the default, but not that fast.

choices.text: Raise the OSPF cost on every cable
choices.why: Cost picks paths; it has nothing to do with noticing a failure.

choices.text: Run BFD alongside OSPF
choices.why: Right. BFD exchanges hellos many times a second, and OSPF reacts to it.

choices.text: Switch from OSPF to RIP
choices.why: RIP waits 180 seconds, far slower.

choices.text: Set a hello of 1 second and a dead interval of 4
choices.why: That is lesson 3's setting, and it detects a silent failure in four seconds.

prompt: The time between a change in the network and every router agreeing on the new paths is called ___.
hint: The routers come together on one answer.

prompt: r1's EIGRP topology shows `via 10.20.0.2 (30720/28160), eth1`. What is 28160?
hint: Whose distance is it?

choices.text: r2's own distance to the network, as r2 reported it
choices.why: Right. It is the reported distance, and r2 is connected to that network.

choices.text: r1's distance through r2
choices.why: That is the first number, 30720.

choices.text: The hold time in milliseconds
choices.why: Hold is in the neighbour table, in seconds.

choices.text: The bandwidth of the eth1 interface, in kilobits per second
choices.why: It is a composite metric, not a bandwidth.

prompt: In r1's EIGRP table, connected networks show FD 28160 and networks one link further show 30720. How much does that one link add?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: Why does r1 have no feasible successor for 10.20.2.0/24 through r4?
hint: Compare r4's reported distance with r1's feasible distance.

choices.text: EIGRP keeps one path per network by design
choices.why: It keeps every offer; the point of the topology table is the backup.

choices.text: r4 reports more than 30720
choices.why: Right. A feasible successor must report less than r1's feasible distance.

choices.text: r4 is not an EIGRP neighbour of r1
choices.why: r4, 10.20.0.13, is in r1's neighbour table on eth4.

choices.text: The OSPF cost of 100 forbids it
choices.why: EIGRP ignores OSPF's cost entirely.

prompt: OSPF sent pc1's traffic round the ring, and EIGRP chose the direct cable to r2. Why the difference?
hint: Where was the 100 configured?

choices.text: EIGRP counts hops, like RIP
choices.why: EIGRP uses bandwidth and delay. Here the interfaces are equal, so fewer links wins, but not by counting hops.

choices.text: EIGRP prefers interfaces with lower numbers
choices.why: Interface names play no part in the metric.

choices.text: The cost of 100 was an OSPF setting, which EIGRP does not read
choices.why: Right. To EIGRP the two interfaces look the same, and the direct path is shorter.

choices.text: EIGRP had not finished converging when the table was read
choices.why: Every route was P, passive: converged.

prompt: Match each protocol to what its metric is made of.
hint: One counts, one adds, one computes.

pairs.right: The number of routers on the path
The sum of a cost on each outgoing interface

right_distractors: The length of the AS path

prompt: Which of these are true of OSPF in this lesson's ring? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the database, the timers and the path.

choices.text: Every router held the same four router LSAs
choices.why: That is link state: one shared map.

choices.text: Traffic from pc1 to pc2 crossed r4 and r3
choices.why: The cost 100 on the direct cable sent it round.

choices.text: A silent failure was noticed in four seconds
choices.why: That was lesson 3's timers. Here the dead interval was 40 seconds.

choices.text: A designated router was elected on each cable
choices.why: The cables were point-to-point, which skips the election.

prompt: A company runs OSPF with default timers across two buildings joined through a media converter. The converter dies but keeps its ports powered. What do users see?
hint: This is the lab's convergence block, in a building.

choices.text: No interruption, since OSPF had a backup path ready
choices.why: OSPF keeps no ready backup; it recalculates after it notices, and noticing is the slow part.

choices.text: Up to about 40 seconds of lost traffic, then service over the other path
choices.why: Right. The dead interval is waited out before OSPF reroutes.

choices.text: A permanent outage until someone replaces the converter
choices.why: OSPF does reroute, once the dead timer expires.

choices.text: A few milliseconds of loss while SPF runs
choices.why: That is the cost when the signal drops. With the signal up, the dead interval comes first.

prompt: In EIGRP, the neighbour currently used for a network is the ___, and a ready backup that meets the feasibility condition is a feasible one.
hint: It comes after you on the way.
